name: pH
scientific_definition: Negative logarithm (base 10) of the hydrogen ion activity: pH = -log10[H+]. Measures acidity or basicity.
environmental_significance: Controls chemical speciation, solubility of heavy metals, effectiveness of coagulation and disinfection, and aquatic habitability.
common_sources: Dissolved CO2, geological mineral dissolution (limestone, carbonates), industrial acid/alkali discharge, acid mine drainage.
relevant_chemistry: Carbonate equilibrium: CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> HCO3- + H+ <-> CO3(2-) + 2H+. Low pH accelerates metal leaching; high pH precipitates calcium carbonate scale.
potential_consequences: Corrosion of water pipes at pH < 6.5 releasing toxic metals (Pb, Cu); bitter taste and encrustation at pH > 8.5; decreased chlorination efficiency at pH > 8.0.

name: Turbidity
scientific_definition: Optical measure of water clarity indicating the degree to which light is scattered by suspended particulate matter.
environmental_significance: Suspended particles shelter pathogens from ultraviolet and chemical disinfection, degrade aesthetic quality, and foul membranes.
common_sources: Soil erosion, surface runoff containing clay and silt, organic matter, algal blooms, colloidal iron/manganese oxides.
relevant_chemistry: Colloidal particles generally possess negative surface charges (zeta potential: -15 to -50 mV), resisting natural settling due to electrostatic repulsion. Coagulation hydrolyzes Al3+ or Fe3+ species to compress the electrical double layer.
potential_consequences: Disinfection shielding, bacterial regrowth in networks, clogging of filtration media, aesthetic rejectability.

name: Total Dissolved Solids
scientific_definition: Aggregate measure of all inorganic salts and small amounts of organic matter dissolved in water.
environmental_significance: Determines electrical conductivity, osmotic pressure, palatability, and scaling/corrosive tendencies.
common_sources: Natural weathering of sedimentary and igneous rock, agricultural runoff, municipal sewage, industrial effluents, road de-icing salts.
relevant_chemistry: Major contributing ions include Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+, K+, HCO3-, SO4(2-), Cl-, and NO3-. Specific conductance relates to TDS via factor ~0.55-0.75 depending on ionic composition.
potential_consequences: Unpalatable mineral taste above 500 mg/L, excessive pipe scaling, gastrointestinal irritation in unaccustomed consumers above 1000 mg/L.

name: Total Hardness
scientific_definition: Concentration of multivalent metallic cations in solution, predominantly calcium (Ca2+) and magnesium (Mg2+), expressed as equivalent CaCO3.
environmental_significance: Influences scale formation in heat transfer systems, soap lathering capacity, and domestic and industrial utility.
common_sources: Dissolution of limestone (CaCO3), dolomite (CaMg(CO3)2), gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O) driven by carbonic acid in soil zones.
relevant_chemistry: Total Hardness = 2.497[Ca, mg/L] + 4.118[Mg, mg/L]. Temporary (carbonate) hardness precipitates on heating: Ca(HCO3)2 -> CaCO3(s) + CO2 + H2O. Permanent (non-carbonate) hardness involves SO4(2-) and Cl-.
potential_consequences: Scale deposition in boilers, geysers, and pipes reducing heat transfer; excessive soap consumption; insoluble curd formation on fixtures.

name: Nitrate
scientific_definition: Highly oxidized inorganic polyatomic nitrogen anion (NO3-) representing the end-stage of aerobic nitrification.
environmental_significance: Primary agricultural contaminant and key driver of eutrophication; critical human health hazard in infants.
common_sources: Synthetic nitrogenous fertilizers (urea, ammonium nitrate), animal feedlots, leaking septic tanks, sewage treatment discharges.
relevant_chemistry: Nitrification: NH4+ + 1.5O2 -> NO2- + 2H+ + H2O (Nitrosomonas), then NO2- + 0.5O2 -> NO3- (Nitrobacter). Highly soluble and mobile in groundwater due to negative charge repelled by negatively charged soil particles.
potential_consequences: Infant methemoglobinemia ('blue baby syndrome') through reduction to nitrite in infant gut binding hemoglobin; linked to potential nitrosamine formation.

name: Chloride
scientific_definition: Monatomic chlorine anion (Cl-) found abundantly in natural waters as dissolved salt components.
environmental_significance: Indicator of seawater intrusion, salinity ingress, or wastewater contamination; critical parameter for corrosion engineering.
common_sources: Halite (NaCl) dissolution, coastal marine intrusion into coastal aquifers, industrial brine discharge, sewage effluents.
relevant_chemistry: Highly conservative tracer in hydrogeology with minimal sorption or biochemical decay. Synergistically accelerates pitting corrosion of stainless steel and copper.
potential_consequences: Salty taste noticeable at >250 mg/L with sodium; accelerated corrosion of metallic plumbing and hot water systems; osmotic stress on plants when used for irrigation.

name: Dissolved Oxygen
scientific_definition: Amount of gaseous non-compound oxygen (O2) dissolved in aqueous solution at equilibrium.
environmental_significance: Crucial indicator of biological water health and self-purification capacity; prevents anaerobic septic odor generation.
common_sources: Atmospheric diffusion and dissolution enhanced by hydraulic turbulence; aquatic plant and algal photosynthesis during daylight.
relevant_chemistry: Solubility governed by Henry's Law: C* = kH * PO2. Saturation concentration decreases with increasing water temperature and salinity (e.g., ~9.1 mg/L at 20 deg C at 1 atm fresh water).
potential_consequences: Depletion (<4 mg/L) causes fish asphyxiation, stimulates anaerobic reduction of sulfate to toxic hydrogen sulfide (H2S), and releases ferrous iron and manganese from sediments.

name: Lead
scientific_definition: Dense, toxic heavy metal element occurring in water as divalent (Pb2+) or complexed aqueous species.
environmental_significance: Potent neurotoxin with bioaccumulative properties and no known safe biological threshold in humans.
common_sources: Corrosion of legacy lead plumbing, lead-soldered copper pipes, brass fixtures, industrial battery recycling, mining runoff.
relevant_chemistry: Solubility increases dramatically at pH < 6.5 or in soft water with low carbonate alkalinity. Forms insoluble basic lead carbonate (hydrocerussite: Pb3(CO3)2(OH)2) in well-buffered alkaline water.
potential_consequences: Irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment in children, lowered IQ, behavioral disorders, hypertension, kidney damage, adult cardiovascular complications.

name: Arsenic
scientific_definition: Naturally occurring toxic metalloid existing primarily in inorganic oxidation states As(III) arsenite and As(V) arsenate.
environmental_significance: Group 1 human carcinogen impacting millions globally through contaminated alluvial aquifers (e.g., Bengal basin, Indus plain).
common_sources: Reductive dissolution of arsenic-bearing iron oxyhydroxides in alluvial aquifers; geothermal springs; pesticide residues; mining tailings.
relevant_chemistry: Speciation is redox and pH dependent: Arsenite (H3AsO3) is uncharged at pH < 9.2 under reducing conditions and much harder to remove; Arsenate (H2AsO4-, HAsO4(2-)) is negatively charged in oxic waters, readily adsorbed on iron hydroxides.
potential_consequences: Chronic arsenicosis, melanosis, keratosis on palms/soles, gangrene ('blackfoot disease'), increased incidence of bladder, lung, and skin cancers.

name: Iron
scientific_definition: Transition metal occurring predominantly in aqueous systems as reduced soluble ferrous (Fe2+) or oxidized insoluble ferric (Fe3+) ions.
environmental_significance: Secondary aesthetic contaminant causing severe discoloration, staining, turbidity, and distribution pipe biofilm encrustation.
common_sources: Dissolution of natural iron-bearing minerals (pyrite, hematite, siderite) in reducing groundwater; corrosion of cast iron/steel mains.
relevant_chemistry: Fe2+ is soluble in anaerobic groundwater. Upon aeration / exposure to atmospheric oxygen: 4Fe2+ + O2 + 10H2O -> 4Fe(OH)3(s) + 8H+. Insoluble ferric hydroxide forms reddish-brown floc.
potential_consequences: Reddish-brown water discoloration, staining of porcelain plumbing and laundry, metallic taste, proliferation of iron bacteria forming slime biofilms.
